newsitem.title: USA: Falling gold prices another boon to US bond market.
newsitem.headline: Falling gold prices another boon to US bond market.

text.p: As if a solid economy, little inflation worries and a Federal Reserve that appears on hold is not enough to cheer the U.S. Treasury market, it now has another reason: plunging gold prices.

Amid the summer doldrums, which have seen volume drop significantly, Treasuries received a lift last week when the Australian central bank said it had dumped much of its gold reserves -- sending prices to a 12-year low -- in favor of owning various government securities.

Gold dove to below $320 an ounce from around $340 in early June and from the mid-$350s in March. Gold prices had jumped to a seven-year high of $420 an ounce in February 1996 before moderating to $367 by the end of the year.
Many experts expect others to follow Austraila's surprising move, as worldwide inflation rates come down.
"Holding a non-interest bearing asset that is deflating in price is a lousy investment," said Paul McCulley, chief economist at UBS Securities LLC.
A number of European central banks, such as the Netherlands and Belgium, already have reduced gold reserves. Canada got the ball rolling back in the late 1970s when it liquidated gold reserves.

According to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York -- where gold is stored for some 50 to 60 central banks other than the U.S., the number of gold bars in its vault has dropped to about 700,000 today from 900,000 10 years ago.

"The question is: do you earn interest on your reserves, which would say hold Treasuries or other (countries') bonds or do you hold gold which doesn't earn interest," asked Larry Dyer, Treasury strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
What Australia and other central banks have done by selling gold reserves was "a vote to earn interest," he added.
Andy Smith, a precious metals analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland in London, said the top 10 central banks "give up $15 billion a year by holding gold rather than holding interest-bearing assets."
He added that clearly, other central banks will increase sales of gold reserves. "It's a matter of who, when and how much," Smith said. "'If' is not in doubt."

Yet, analysts do not believe the impact on U.S. Treasuries will be noticeable from a flow-of-funds standpoint, since the amount of securities bought is miniscule in the overall market. For example, Austraila sold less than $2.0 billion in gold and that has to be spread among numerous bond markets.
Other central banks might decide against Treasuries, so it is tough to determine the monetary effects from gold sales.
Therefore, Treasuries benefit from the psychology of falling gold prices, since lower gold prices suggest confidence that inflation will remain subdued.

"Inflation has gone out of style and that's great for Treasuries," said John Ryding, senior economist at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc. "What gold is telling us is people are buying into the lower-inflation outlook."
And it is not just in the U.S.
"Central banks everywhere are against inflation," Ryding said. "(The fall in gold prices) tells you that there is not much of a problem on that front."
